checks: For an interior point, any containing halfspace whose boundary misses y loses positive simplex volume when tightened to y: a small ball about y lies in the simplex and supplies an open piece of the removed strip. Normal continuity follows by dominated convergence across volume-null boundaries; compactness gives a minimizing through-y halfspace. Every such through-interior cut is proper. The stationary-cap predecessor thus gives one strict included vertex for d≥2; for d=1 this is automatic.

For the unique strictly included vertex i, the intercept fraction satisfies 0<tⱼ≤1, and λⱼ(x)/tⱼ are the barycentric weights of the intercepts in the cap simplex. The normalized determinant is ∏tⱼ. The point y lies on its boundary exactly when ∑λⱼ/tⱼ=1. This includes tⱼ=1, meaning vertex j lies on the boundary rather than strictly included.

At μᵢ=d every water-level contribution is λⱼ/(dλⱼ)=1/d, including ties at one. There must be some tⱼ<1 since λᵢ>0, so the constructed halfspace is proper. As an independent lower-bound and equality check, AM–GM applied to the d positive terms λⱼ/tⱼ of sum one gives ∏tⱼ≥d^d∏λⱼ with equality precisely when every tⱼ=dλⱼ. Minimizing the products is equivalent to maximizing the omitted positive coordinate; tied maximizers produce distinct halfspaces with their own unique strict vertex.

Exactly two nonzero margins cannot be overlooked in the global argument: such a proper cut already has one strict included vertex, and the same optimization applies. If it achieved the fixed-vertex optimum with d≥2, its d−1 other zero margins would force d−1 coordinates to equal 1/d. The two remaining coordinates are positive and sum to 1/d, so the included vertex cannot maximize λ. It is therefore not a global minimizer.

A zero-volume containing halfspace cannot meet int(T), since an interior ball meets either side of any plane through its center in positive volume. Closure then puts T on the opposite closed side, and y lies on the supporting boundary. Conversely every outward supporting halfspace through y has zero volume. Under the central bound a boundary point has exactly one zero coordinate and all d others equal 1/d, so it is a facet centroid. For d=1 the formula is min(λ₀,λ₁), with the two midpoint choices and the outward endpoint halfspaces included.
